source.name: SB9: The ninth catalogue of spectroscopic binary orbits (Pourbaix et al. 2004, 2004A&A...424..727P)
source.frozenFiles: catalog-work/star-systems/sb9-20240621 (Main.dta, Orbits.dta, Alias.dta, ReadMe.txt; Notes.dta not retained)

policy: A double-lined SB9 orbit measures both stars, so it establishes both components. A single-lined orbit establishes an unseen companion of unknown nature, which may be a white dwarf or a substellar object; it is authored only with a published SB9 component spectrum or a reviewed classification below. Other single-lined systems remain pending review.

567.evidence: Abstract: "We detect a main sequence B star companion and rule out the compact object scenario."

782.evidence: Abstract: "the secondary components are pre-MS stars, in the process of contracting onto the MS." Table 7 gives only model ranges (M2 0.59-1.45 Msun), so no individual value is adopted.

940.source: Strassmeier et al. 2012 Table 4 SB1 orbit (P = 39.48042 +/- 0.00012 d, K = 31.849 +/- 0.013 km/s, e = 0, f(M) = 0.1325 Msun); Bale et al. 2025 primary mass 3.50 Msun; eclipsing binary (Avvakumova et al. 2013, 2013AN....334..860A)
940.reasoning: With the 3.50 Msun primary and an edge-on eclipsing orbit, f(M) = 0.1325 Msun requires a companion of about 1.5 Msun, above the white-dwarf mass limit. Hinderer (1957), quoted in the Strassmeier et al. 2012 notes, classified it as a dA8-dF0 dwarf; that classification was not verified verbatim and is not adopted as a spectral type.

1081.evidence: Abstract: "including the first detection of the companion of $\beta$ Scuti with precise relative astrometry"; a resolved optical companion is luminous. The far-UV B9 type (Parsons & Ake 1998) was not verified and is not adopted.

1106.evidence: Table 4 (this study): K1 = 36.4 (0.05) km/s, K2 = 273.7 (0.05) km/s. The secondary's lines are measured, so this contact binary is double-lined in current data; SB9 lists only K1.

1306.source: Escorza & De Rosa 2023, A&A 671, A97, 'Barium and related stars, and their white-dwarf companions III. The masses of the white dwarfs'
1306.evidence: Table 2 row: "HD 204075 | 2367 ±9 | 0.26 ±0.05 | ... | 133 ±5 | 0.67 ±0.10 | ..." with column MWD = 0.67 ± 0.10 Msun from the combined RV/astrometric orbit.

1331.evidence: Abstract: "The secondary was detected with a K band flux ratio 6.0% ± 0.2%, confirming it is a red dwarf"; footnote: the eclipse "could not be explained by a white dwarf companion". Model-based mass/radius/temperature (M ≃ 0.65 Msun) are approximate and not adopted.

1546.evidence: Table 1 row for HD 13611 (Xi1 Cet): white-dwarf companion mass 0.80 Msun, a = 3.8 au, P = 4.50 yr. The DA4 class (McCook & Sion 1999) was not verified and is not adopted.

2446.source: Gratton et al. 2023, A&A 678, A93 (SPHERE imaging)
2446.evidence: Appendix A, HIP 62434: imaged companion "projected at about 0.1 arcsec (about 9 au) from the star ... (M=1.9±0.07 M⊙)" and "It is then reasonable to identify AB as the responsible of the RV variations" of the 5-yr Aerts et al. (1998) orbit. Photometric mass not adopted.

3013.source: Frozen SIMBAD composite classification M8.5+T5 for 2MASS J03202839-0446358 (catalog-work/nearest-5000/simbad.csv); SB9 orbit 2008ApJ...678L.125B
3013.evidence: SB9 Main.dta lists component spectra M8|G0. A G0 star cannot be the unseen companion of this late-M dwarf; the SB9 secondary type is rejected and never shipped. Component spectra follow the SIMBAD composite: M8.5 primary and T5 brown-dwarf secondary.

B.reason: Inconsistent with the M8.5+T5 composite classification of the same object.

A.reason: Superseded by the finer M8.5 composite classification.

3221.evidence: Abstract: "evidence for a white dwarf as its dark and unseen companion". Section 4: 0.50 +0.03/-0.04 Msun from the mass function and the Hipparcos astrometric inclination; the Rappaport et al. (1995) period relation predicts 0.48 Msun.

exclusions.396: The SB9 orbit is the A0620-00 black-hole binary. Its visible star is component B of the reviewed compact system a0620-00-system; the unseen component is the black hole already in the compact overlay.
exclusions.552: The SB9 orbit is the Vela X-1 binary. Its visible star HD 77581 is component B of the reviewed compact system vela-x-1-system; the unseen component is the neutron star already in the compact overlay.

nakedEyePolicy: Naked-eye rows admitted to the companion pool: 49 Lib by review, plus every double-lined SB9 system whose exact identity matches one otherwise single naked-eye row and whose SB9 entry is the whole star or its A component.

nakedEyeHeld.hip-20284: HD 27483: SB9 gives an F6V + F6V close pair, while the SIMBAD composite DA3+F6V describes the white dwarf elsewhere in the system. The composite-spectrum rule would make the primary a white dwarf, so it needs a reviewed hierarchy.
